While there are certainly some languages that are more marketable than others, languages change over time and fairly quickly. For example, writing apps for Apple devices used to be done in Objective C, and now Apple has their own language called Swift. I would recommend that you learn a few algorithms with some pseudo-code just to get good at picking up any language. javascript in codecademy is an amazing lesson. I was there for hours without noticing time gone by. I find it engaging and fun. I mean, lol making a rock paper scissors game in the first 2 hours was pretty awesome.

You could pick up ruby, it's a very simple language (I like it more than python). To gain familiarity with the language you choose, you should either try Code Katas or Project Euler. The exercises are mostly easy enough for a beginner to solve, and if you do enough if them, you'll eventually get 'good enough' at the language that you can solve real problems.

A lot of people recommend weakly-typed (you can look up what that means) languages like Python and Ruby, but I find having a compiler give you error messages can be a great learning tool. I'm a big C# fan but Java is also nice, especially if you're on Linux. Mono probably works well but I have no experience with it.

I personally started with C when I entered college. It introduces you to a lot of things at once, though. I used Programming for the Scientifically Inclined and The C Programming Language as books I worked through on my own. It really helped me understand the C and MATLAB courses I had to take as part of my engineering degree.

I personally love C as I have not had any problem learning other languages (C++, Python, Minitab) by having that as my foundation.

My personal opinion would be to start with Python. It's relatively easy to pick up fast, and even the tutorial on the website is really good. This is what I did when I first started and I think it taught me a lot about programming in general. It is weakly typed, as someone else mentioned, which means that it will more than likely be easier to get started on, but you will have more to learn when you move to a language like C++ or Java.

I wouldn't start with C++ as you'll need to learn a lot about memory management and that sort of stuff along with general programming concepts, but that may not be a bad thing in a way.

In the end though, it doesn't make too much of a difference which language you start with as you are basically just picking up skills that will be applied to whichever language you end up using later on. After all, a programming language (or even a language in general) is just a tool used to express your ideas, not a restriction on your ideas themselves. Whichever you choose, make sure you don't just learn the theory and actually get a lot of practice. I used to make up random little projects for myself when I started which probably helped me to get the programming knowledge I have now.

Everyone is going to have a differing opinion about their favorite starter language and it will at least in part depend on their personal experience, the languages they have or have not been exposed to, and the reasons they got into programming.

A CS course in college may start you with machine code, or C++, or Python. Not because any of these have anything specifically in common but because the class has a goal. It is meant to teach you to accomplish a task or set of tasks using that language. And the languages are chosen because they are well established, well documented and oft used.

I would say the best place to start is by asking yourself what it is you want to do. What type of programs do you want to write? Mobile Apps? Video Games? Web Sites? Desktop Applications? And then find a path that leads there. Now many of the languages out there can do many, if not all, of those things. So figure out what you want to do, and from there your friends here will be able to shape a more helpful suggestion!

That aside, personally, I use Python to teach people who have never done programming before, but given you experience with C++, I would strongly recommend C#. The .net aspect takes a lot of the troublesome/tedious parts of programming in C++ out of the equation, and while the syntax is not 1:1 most of the keywords you know will still be around and it may be an easier transition.

I am very pro-vaccination, but I don't mind students taking controversial classes to broaden their horizons. They just need to take it with a grain of salt and hopefully don't take the literal concepts of "don't vaccinate children." It's important to learn both sides of the argument, even when science proves one side is wrong.

I do wholeheartedly agree that people need to be exposed to both sides, as it allows educated defense against whichever side you oppose. My concern with this is that an establishment of higher learning is allowing this course with lackluster resources. The information provided to students should be of published work (that is credited), or resources that have some backing (in this case scientifically or even historically)

There's a difference, though, between teaching controversial material (i.e. material that is unpopular or part of a marginal field) and teaching material which doesn't seem to have any scientific backing whatsoever, particularly when the professor doesn't seem to have any relevant experience in (for example) quantum physics. Likewise, we can reasonably separate teaching something (e.g. Theology) from teaching about something (e.g. Religious Studies): the latter would have been fine here, but it seems as though it was far more the former.

From Wikipedia

Fixed science/engineering instruments include:

Panoramic Camera (Pancam) – examines the texture, color, mineralogy, and structure of the local terrain.

Navigation Camera (Navcam) – monochrome with a higher field of view but lower resolution, for navigation and driving.

Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer (Mini-TES) – identifies promising rocks and soils for closer examination, and determines the processes that formed them.

Hazcams, two B&W cameras with 120 degree field of view, that provide additional data about the rover's surroundings.

The rover arm holds the following instruments:

Mössbauer spectrometer (MB) MIMOS II – used for close-up investigations of the mineralogy of iron-bearing rocks and soils.

Alpha particle X-ray spectrometer (APXS) – close-up analysis of the abundances of elements that make up rocks and soils.

Magnets – for collecting magnetic dust particles

Microscopic Imager (MI) – obtains close-up, high-resolution images of rocks and soils.

Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT) – exposes fresh material for examination by instruments on board.

The cameras produce 1024-pixel by 1024-pixel images, the data is compressed with ICER, stored, and transmitted later.
